turns.t: Today we're going to look at an animal with a very unusual way of surviving the winter: the wood frog. Wood frogs live in North America, as far north as Alaska, where winter temperatures can drop far below freezing. Most frogs survive the cold by hiding at the bottom of ponds, where the water doesn't freeze. But the wood frog stays on land, under a layer of dead leaves, and it actually lets its body freeze.

When ice starts to form on its skin, the frog's liver quickly sends large amounts of sugar into its blood. This sugar works a bit like the antifreeze people put in their cars. It protects the inside of the frog's cells, so ice forms only in the spaces around them. Up to about two-thirds of the water in the frog's body can turn to ice. Its heart stops beating, and it stops breathing.

For weeks, the frog is as hard as a rock. Then, when spring arrives and the ground warms up, the frog thaws. Its heart starts beating again, and within a day or so, it hops away to find a pond. Scientists are studying wood frogs because what they learn might one day help doctors keep human organs fresh for longer before transplants.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
o: How cars are protected from ice
How the wood frog survives being frozen
Where frogs find food in winter
questions.why: The whole talk explains how the wood frog freezes in winter and comes back to life in spring.

questions.q: Where does the wood frog spend the winter?
o: At the bottom of a pond
In a hole in a tree
questions.why: "The wood frog stays on land, under a layer of dead leaves."

questions.q: What does the sugar in the frog's blood do?
o: It gives the frog energy to hop
It keeps the frog's heart beating
It helps the frog find a pond
It stops ice from forming inside its cells
questions.why: The sugar protects the inside of the cells, so ice forms only around them.

questions.q: Why are scientists interested in wood frogs?

They might learn how to keep organs fresh for transplants
They want to make better antifreeze for cars
They need to count the frogs in Alaska
questions.why: What they learn might help doctors keep human organs fresh for longer before transplants.

turns.t: Imagine you ruled a huge empire in the mountains, with no phones, no horses and no written letters. How would you send a message? About five hundred years ago, the Inca Empire in South America faced exactly this problem. Their solution was a team of runners called chasquis.

The Inca built thousands of kilometers of roads through the Andes. Along these roads, every few kilometers, there were small stations where chasquis waited. When a runner arrived with a message, he repeated it to the next runner, who then raced to the following station. Because each chasqui ran only a short distance at top speed, a message could travel about two hundred and forty kilometers in a single day.

But how did the chasquis carry information like numbers, if the Inca did not write? They used a quipu, a set of colored strings with knots tied in them. The color of a string and the position of each knot showed numbers, such as how much corn was stored in a town. Today, only a few hundred quipus survive in museums, and researchers are still trying to understand all of them.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
o: How messages were sent across the Inca Empire
How the Inca built their roads
Why the Inca did not use horses
How corn was grown in the Andes
questions.why: The talk explains the chasqui runners and the quipus they carried.

questions.q: Why could messages travel so quickly?
o: The runners rode horses on flat roads
The messages were sent by fire signals
Each runner ran only a short distance very fast
questions.why: "Because each chasqui ran only a short distance at top speed..."

questions.q: What was a quipu used for?
o: Marking the stations along the road
questions.why: The color and position of the knots showed numbers.

o: They are still used in the Andes
Most of them were lost by runners
Researchers do not fully understand all of them

questions.why: "Researchers are still trying to understand all of them."

turns.t: Today let's talk about one of the ocean's best hiders: the octopus. An octopus has no shell and no bones, so many animals would love to eat it. To stay safe, it can change the color of its skin in less than a second, matching the rocks, sand or coral around it.

How does it do this? Its skin contains thousands of tiny bags of color called chromatophores. Each bag is surrounded by small muscles. When the muscles pull, the bag stretches open and the color spreads out, like a drop of paint. When they relax, the bag closes and the color almost disappears. An octopus can also change the texture of its skin, making little bumps that look like the surface of a rock.

Here's the strange part. Scientists believe that most octopuses are colorblind. So how do they match colors they can't see? Nobody knows for sure. Some researchers think their skin itself may be able to sense light. It's one of the mysteries scientists are still trying to solve.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
o: How octopuses change color to hide
questions.why: The talk explains how and why the octopus changes its color and skin.

questions.why: "When the muscles pull, the bag stretches open and the color spreads out."

questions.q: Besides color, what else can an octopus change?
questions.why: It can make little bumps that look like the surface of a rock.

questions.q: What is surprising about octopuses?

questions.why: "Scientists believe that most octopuses are colorblind. So how do they match colors they can't see?"

turns.t: Think about how much paper you use every day: notebooks, books, tickets, even the receipt at the store. But for most of history, people wrote on other things, like clay, animal skins or silk. Clay was heavy, skins took a long time to prepare, and silk was very expensive.

About two thousand years ago, around the year one hundred and five, a Chinese official named Cai Lun improved a way of making paper. He mixed tree bark, old cloth and even old fishing nets with water, and pounded them into a soft paste. Then he spread the paste thinly on a screen and let it dry. The result was light, cheap and easy to write on.

For hundreds of years, the Chinese kept the method mostly to themselves. Paper-making slowly spread to Korea and Japan, and later to the Arab world, where cities like Baghdad built paper mills. From there, it finally reached Europe, almost a thousand years after Cai Lun. Without this invention, printed books, and maybe even schools as we know them, would have arrived much later.

questions.why: The talk describes Cai Lun's paper and how it spread around the world.

questions.why: Clay was heavy, skins took a long time to prepare, and silk was very expensive.

questions.why: "Without this invention, printed books, and maybe even schools as we know them, would have arrived much later."

turns.t: Here in Colombia, in the Serranía de la Macarena in the department of Meta, there is a river that many people call the most beautiful in the world. Its name is Caño Cristales, but it is also known as the river of five colors.

The water itself isn't colored. In fact, it's extremely clear. The colors come from a plant that grows on the rocks at the bottom of the river. When there's the right amount of water and sunlight, this plant turns bright red and pink. Together with yellow sand, green moss, blue water and black rocks, it creates a rainbow under the surface.

But you can't see the colors all year. In the dry season, there's too little water, and the plant stops growing. In the heaviest part of the rainy season, the water is too deep and fast for enough sunlight to reach the plant. The best time to visit is usually between June and November. To protect the river, visitors must go with a local guide, and sunscreen and insect repellent are not allowed in the water, because the chemicals can harm the plant.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
o: How rivers are formed in mountains
Why a Colombian river looks colorful at certain times
Why the Meta region is dry
questions.why: The talk explains Caño Cristales, where its colors come from and when they can be seen.

questions.q: Where do the red colors come from?
o: A plant growing on the rocks
questions.why: "The colors come from a plant that grows on the rocks at the bottom of the river."

o: Not enough sunlight reaches the plant through the deep, fast water

turns.t: Every year, billions of birds fly thousands of kilometers between their summer and winter homes. Some small birds that spend the summer in North America fly all the way to Colombia and beyond. And many of them make this trip alone, at night, for the very first time. So how do they find their way?

Scientists have found that birds use several tools at once. During the day, they use the position of the sun, like a compass. At night, many birds use the stars. In one famous experiment, young birds were raised in a planetarium, a building where the stars are shown on the ceiling. When the scientists changed the position of the stars, the birds changed the direction they tried to fly.

Birds can also sense the Earth's magnetic field, something humans can't feel at all. And as they get closer to home, they recognize landmarks like rivers, coastlines and mountains. Some birds may even use smell. Because they have so many tools, a cloudy night doesn't stop them. If one tool doesn't work, they use another.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
o: Why birds fly south in winter
What birds eat on long trips
How migrating birds find their way
questions.why: The talk explains the different tools birds use to navigate.

questions.q: What did the planetarium experiment show?
o: Birds use the stars to choose a direction
Birds prefer to fly in groups
Birds remember the buildings they see
questions.why: When the stars were moved, the birds changed direction.

questions.q: What can birds sense that humans cannot?
questions.why: "Birds can also sense the Earth's magnetic field, something humans can't feel at all."

questions.q: Why doesn't a cloudy night stop migrating birds?
o: Clouds help them see the stars
They can use another tool when one does not work
They wait for the sun to come out
questions.why: "If one tool doesn't work, they use another."

Leave their instruments next to the door

turns.t: Starting this week, the library has two areas. The tables near the windows are now a quiet zone, for students who need to read or study alone. Please don't talk there at all. If you're working on a group project, you can use the round tables near the computers, where talking in a low voice is fine. This way, everyone can find a place that works for them.

questions.q: Where should students go to work on a group project?
o: To the tables near the windows
To the round tables near the computers
questions.why: "If you're working on a group project, you can use the round tables near the computers."

turns.t: Each of you now has a bean plant in a cup. For the next two weeks, you'll keep a plant journal. Every morning, measure the height of your plant in centimeters and write it in your journal. Also write one sentence about how it looks. Water it only on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays. Too much water is just as bad as too little.

questions.q: How often should students water their plants?
questions.why: "Water it only on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays."

turns.t: Valeria, have you heard from Daniela? She wasn't in class today.
She texted me. She has a bad cold and will probably be out until Thursday.
Oh no. Our presentation is on Wednesday! She was going to talk about the history part.
I know. But she sent me her notes and the slides last night, so we have everything we need.
Okay. Then one of us has to learn her part. Can you do it? You're better at history than me.
Fine, but then you have to write the questions for the end of the presentation.
Deal. And let's ask Mr. Ortiz if Daniela can present her part separately when she comes back, so she still gets a grade.
Good idea. Let's talk to him after lunch.

questions.q: What is the students' problem?
o: A group member is sick before their presentation
questions.why: Daniela has a bad cold and the presentation is on Wednesday.

questions.q: What will Valeria do?
questions.why: Mateo asks her to learn Daniela's history part and she agrees.

questions.q: Why do they want to talk to Mr. Ortiz?
o: To ask if Daniela can present her part later
questions.why: "Let's ask Mr. Ortiz if Daniela can present her part separately when she comes back."

items.type: Phone conversation · student and bike shop

turns.t: Good morning, Rueda Libre Bike Shop.
Hi. I'm calling about my bike. I brought it in on Monday because the brakes weren't working. Is it ready?
Let me check. What's your name?
Leo Martínez.
Yes, here it is. The brakes are fixed, but our mechanic also noticed that your back tire is very worn. It could get a hole soon.
Oh. How much would a new tire cost?
Forty thousand pesos, including the work. We could have it ready by this afternoon.
Hmm, I only have thirty thousand with me. Can I pay the rest on Saturday?
That's fine. We'll change the tire, and you can pick up the bike today after four.

questions.q: Why did Leo take his bike to the shop?
questions.why: "I brought it in on Monday because the brakes weren't working."

questions.q: What did the mechanic notice?
o: The back tire is very worn
The bike is too small for Leo
questions.why: "Our mechanic also noticed that your back tire is very worn."

questions.q: What will Leo probably do on Saturday?
o: Bring his bike back to fix the brakes
Pay the rest of the money
questions.why: He picks up the bike today and asks to pay the rest on Saturday.

turns.t: Look at the Moon on different nights, and it seems to change shape. Sometimes it's a full circle, sometimes a half, and sometimes just a thin smile. Many people think this happens because the Earth's shadow covers part of the Moon. But that's not true.

The Moon doesn't make its own light. We see it because sunlight reflects off its surface. At every moment, half of the Moon is lit by the Sun, just as half of the Earth is in daytime. As the Moon travels around the Earth, which takes about twenty-nine and a half days, we see different amounts of that lit half.

When the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun, the lit side faces away from us, and we can hardly see the Moon at all. We call that a new moon. When the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, we see the whole lit side: a full moon. The Earth's shadow only falls on the Moon during a lunar eclipse, and that happens just a few times a year.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
o: Why the Moon makes its own light
Why the Moon seems to change shape
How to watch a lunar eclipse
questions.why: The talk explains the real reason for the Moon's phases.

questions.q: What common belief does the speaker say is wrong?
o: That the Earth's shadow causes the Moon's phases
That the Moon travels around the Earth
That sunlight reflects off the Moon
That half of the Moon is always lit
questions.why: "Many people think this happens because the Earth's shadow covers part of the Moon. But that's not true."

questions.q: How long does the Moon take to go around the Earth?
o: About twenty-nine and a half days
questions.why: "Which takes about twenty-nine and a half days."

questions.q: What happens during a new moon?
o: The Earth's shadow covers the Moon
The Moon is behind the Earth
The lit side of the Moon faces away from Earth
questions.why: "When the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun, the lit side faces away from us."

turns.t: Before 1914, a ship sailing from New York to San Francisco had to travel all the way around the southern tip of South America. The trip was more than twenty thousand kilometers long and could take months. Then the Panama Canal opened, and the journey became less than half as long.

Building the canal was extremely difficult. A French company tried first, in the 1880s, but it gave up after thousands of workers died, mainly from diseases like malaria and yellow fever, which are spread by mosquitoes. When the United States took over the project in 1904, doctors drained swamps and used nets and screens to control the mosquitoes. Only then could the work continue safely.

Another challenge was the land itself. Panama is not flat, so engineers built a system of locks. Locks are like giant water elevators. A ship enters a chamber, the gates close, and water flows in until the ship has risen about twenty-six meters to a lake in the middle of the country. On the other side, more locks lower it back down to the ocean. Today, more than twelve thousand ships pass through the canal every year.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
o: Why ships travel to San Francisco
The history of New York's port
How and why the Panama Canal was built
questions.why: The talk explains why the canal was needed and the problems in building it.

questions.q: Why did the French company give up?
o: Thousands of workers died from diseases
questions.why: "It gave up after thousands of workers died, mainly from diseases like malaria and yellow fever."

questions.q: What does the speaker compare locks to?
questions.why: "Locks are like giant water elevators."

questions.q: What can be inferred about the canal?
o: It is no longer used today
It saves ships a lot of time
It was finished by the French
questions.why: The journey became less than half as long, and thousands of ships still use it.

turns.t: Tomorrow is our trip to the botanical garden. We'll leave at eight and come back around three. There's no restaurant at the garden, so you need to bring your own lunch. Please don't bring anything in glass bottles, because they can break on the bus. Also, the garden doesn't have many trash cans, so bring a plastic bag to take your trash home with you.

questions.q: Why should students bring a plastic bag?
o: To carry plants from the garden
questions.why: "Bring a plastic bag to take your trash home with you."

turns.t: Good morning, everyone. Next Friday, the library is holding its first book swap. Bring up to three books you have already read, and you can exchange them for books that other students bring. All books must be in good condition, with no missing pages. Books for very young children won't be accepted, because this event is for students in grades six to nine.

questions.q: What can students do at the book swap?
o: Buy books at a low price
Exchange books they have read for other books
Return library books late without paying
questions.why: "Bring up to three books you have already read, and you can exchange them for books that other students bring."

turns.t: Good news, team. Our new uniforms have arrived! They're blue and white, and each one has your number on the back. Please try yours on today and tell me by Friday if it's the wrong size. After Friday, I can't change them. And remember, the uniforms are only for games, not for practice, so please keep them clean and bring them back after every match.

questions.q: What must players do by Friday?
o: Say if their uniform is the wrong size
questions.why: "Tell me by Friday if it's the wrong size. After Friday, I can't change them."

turns.t: As you can see, we now have our own weather station on the school roof. It measures the temperature, the rain and the wind speed every fifteen minutes and sends the information to this computer. Each week, two students will be in charge of reading the data and writing a short weather report for the school newspaper. I'll put the schedule on the door, so you know when it's your turn.

questions.q: What will two students do each week?
o: Write a weather report for the school newspaper
questions.why: They will read the data and write a short weather report for the school newspaper.

turns.t: Your report cards will be ready next Tuesday. This year, they won't be printed. Instead, your parents will receive an email with a link and a password. If your parents don't have an email address, or if they don't receive the message, please let me know before Tuesday, and I'll print a copy for them. Parent-teacher meetings will be on Thursday afternoon.

questions.q: What should students do if their parents do not have an email address?
o: Go to the meeting on Thursday
Print the report card at home
questions.why: "Please let me know before Tuesday, and I'll print a copy for them."

turns.t: Today you'll create a new password for your school account. A good password has at least ten characters and mixes letters, numbers and symbols. Don't use your name, your birthday or the name of your pet, because those are easy to guess. And never share your password with a friend, even your best friend. If you forget it, come and see me, and I'll reset it.

questions.q: Why shouldn't students use their birthday as a password?
o: The computer does not accept numbers
questions.why: "Don't use your name, your birthday or the name of your pet, because those are easy to guess."

turns.t: Leo, what are you doing on Saturday morning?
Nothing much. Why?
I'm volunteering at the animal shelter near the park. They need people to walk the dogs and clean the cages. Do you want to come?
I'd love to, but I'm a little afraid of big dogs.
That's okay. You could help with the cats instead. They need someone to play with them and give them their food.
That sounds perfect. Do we need to bring anything?
Just old clothes. And you need a form signed by your parents, because we're under sixteen.
No problem. I'll ask my mom tonight.

questions.q: What does Maya invite Leo to do?
questions.why: "I'm volunteering at the animal shelter near the park. Do you want to come?"

questions.q: Why is Leo unsure at first?
o: He is afraid of big dogs
questions.why: "I'm a little afraid of big dogs."

questions.q: Why does Leo need a form signed by his parents?
o: He wants to adopt a cat
questions.why: "You need a form signed by your parents, because we're under sixteen."

turns.t: Ms. Park, do you have a minute? I wanted to ask about the debate team.
Of course, Valeria. Are you thinking of joining?
Yes, but I'm not sure I'm good enough. I get nervous when I speak in front of people.
Almost everyone does at first. That's actually one of the reasons the team exists: to help students become more confident.
How often do you meet?
Every Tuesday after school, for an hour and a half. Before a competition, we sometimes add a Saturday practice.
And do I have to try out?
No tryouts. Just come next Tuesday and watch. If you like it, you can join.

questions.q: Why is Valeria unsure about joining the debate team?
o: She has no time on Tuesdays
She gets nervous speaking in front of people
questions.why: "I get nervous when I speak in front of people."

questions.q: When does the team sometimes practice on Saturdays?
questions.why: "Before a competition, we sometimes add a Saturday practice."

questions.q: What does Ms. Park suggest that Valeria do?
o: Talk to the other members first
questions.why: "Just come next Tuesday and watch."

turns.t: Camels can survive in deserts where temperatures go above forty-five degrees and there may be no water for weeks. Many people believe that a camel's hump is full of water. In fact, it's full of fat. When food is hard to find, the camel's body uses this fat for energy. A hungry camel's hump can even become soft and fall to one side.

So how do camels manage without water? First, when they do find water, they can drink an enormous amount very quickly, around a hundred liters in about ten minutes. Second, they lose very little water. Their bodies can heat up during the day without sweating, and then cool down at night. Their noses also catch moisture from the air they breathe out.

Camels have other desert tools, too. Long eyelashes and nostrils that can close protect them from sandstorms. Wide, soft feet keep them from sinking into the sand. And their tough mouths let them eat thorny plants that most other animals avoid.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
o: How camels are able to survive in the desert
questions.why: The talk describes the hump, water use and other features that help camels survive.

questions.q: What is inside a camel's hump?
questions.why: "Many people believe that a camel's hump is full of water. In fact, it's full of fat."

questions.q: How do camels lose very little water?
o: They don't sweat during the day, and their noses catch moisture
They always stay in the shade
questions.why: Their bodies heat up without sweating, and their noses catch moisture from their breath.

questions.q: Why don't camels sink into the sand?
questions.why: "Wide, soft feet keep them from sinking into the sand."

turns.t: Think of French fries, potato chips or a bowl of ajiaco. Potatoes are now one of the most important foods in the world. But for most of history, people outside South America had never seen one. The potato was first grown in the Andes, near Lake Titicaca, between Peru and Bolivia, about eight thousand years ago.

The people of the Andes developed thousands of different kinds of potatoes, in many colors and shapes. They also found a clever way to store them. They left the potatoes outside on freezing nights and then stepped on them during the sunny days to squeeze out the water. The result, called chuño, could be kept for years without going bad.

In the 1500s, Spanish sailors brought potatoes to Europe. At first, many Europeans didn't trust them. Some thought they caused disease, and others grew the plants only as decoration in their gardens. But farmers slowly discovered that potatoes grew well in cold places and produced more food from the same land than wheat. Within two hundred years, potatoes had become a basic food in many European countries.

questions.q: What is the talk mainly about?
o: The history of the potato and how it spread
questions.why: The talk goes from the first potatoes in the Andes to their arrival in Europe.

questions.q: Where were potatoes first grown?
o: In the Andes, near Lake Titicaca
questions.why: "The potato was first grown in the Andes, near Lake Titicaca."

questions.q: What was chuño?
o: Potatoes dried so they could be stored
questions.why: Frozen at night and squeezed in the sun, chuño could be kept for years.

questions.q: Why did European farmers finally accept potatoes?
o: Potatoes grew well in cold places and gave a lot of food
questions.why: "Potatoes grew well in cold places and produced more food from the same land than wheat."
